newsitem.title: USA: Kellogg profits hurt by cereal price wars.
newsitem.headline: Kellogg profits hurt by cereal price wars.

text.p: Kellogg Co., the nation's largest cereal manufacturer, said Friday its earnings tumbled by 24 percent in the first quarter as last year's price cuts continued to hurt its profit margins.
Looking ahead, the domestic cereal giant, which makes Rice Krispies and Corn Flakes, said it expects earnings and sales growth to resume in the second quarter.
Analysts said the company's second-quarter results face an easy comparison with depressed year-ago earnings, which fell 42 percent from the prior period.
"We can look forward now to a couple of up quarters ... on very easy comparisons," Goldman Sachs analyst Nomi Ghez said.
Kellogg's net income for the three months ended March 31 slid to $160.6 million from $206.1 million in the first quarter of 1996.
Earnings per share dropped to 77 cents a share from 99 cents, a 22 percent decline, with fewer shares outstanding in the current period from a year ago.
Revenues shrank 5.4 percent to $1.69 billion from $1.79 billion, although global sales volume rose 10 percent, including the Lender's bagel business that was acquired in December.
Excluding Lender's, the Battle Creek, Mich.-based company said its global sales volume was up 3 percent.

"We faced a difficult year-to-year comparison in the first quarter, and this was the last of four quarterly comparisons heavily influenced by the 1996 cereal price reductions in the United States," Kellogg Chairman Arnold Langbo said.
"Still, our overall performance was encouraging, with particularly strong sales growth in cereal in Asia and Latin America and in convenience foods in North America," he added.
Langbo said U.S. cereal volume sales improved late in the quarter and was continuing to grow in April, with market share improvement in both the United States and Britain.

He said the company was pleased with the performance of its two newest cereals in the United States, Kellogg's Honey Crunch Corn Flakes, introduced last fall, and Kellogg's Cocoa Frosted Flakes, which was rolled out in March.
Analysts estimated Kellogg's domestic cereal volume fell about two percent in the first quarter, while international volume was up about 2 percent.
Kellogg's stock rose 62.5 cents to $66.625 in consolidated afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
"There may be a sense that the worst is over," BT Securities analyst John O'Neil said. "Starting next quarter, Kellogg should start generating earnings per share increases."
